## Definitions

- [statement] PrintNinja’s dated USD benchmark is a 54-card poker deck with a printed tuck box on Blue Core 280 gsm: $2.69 per deck at 500 decks ($1,343 total) and $1.94 at 1,000 ($1,943 total). These are rounded displayed unit prices; use the quoted order totals for budgeting. This benchmark is not a quote for a larger game. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-02) — https://printninja.com/printing-prices/card-game-printing/ · keywords: Card game manufacturing route choice and production economics · also: https://printninja.com/printing-products/card-game-printing/

## Structure and components

- [statement] PrintNinja’s help page contains inconsistent shipping estimates: its card-specific answer gives 6–8 weeks shipping after 3–4 weeks printing, while its general answer gives five weeks standard ocean shipping. Preserve both attributed estimates and confirm a project schedule. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-06) — https://printninja.com/help/
- [statement] Panda says it includes spare components for customer replacement requests. This is a manufacturer support provision, not a measured transit damage rate. Replacement stock and reshipment expenses need separate project assumptions. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-06) — https://pandagm.com/our-process/
- [statement] The Game Crafter says to enter the total card count of a type across decks when building a quote; its example combines two decks of 20 poker cards as 40 cards. That quote omits stock components and cutting charges for certain custom-cut products, so those omissions need separate cost entries when applicable. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-01-22) — https://help.thegamecrafter.com/article/23-game-costs
- [statement] The Game Crafter labels its card components as priced by the sheet and warns that displayed component prices are configurable examples. The cached pricing table contains unresolved template expressions, so it does not establish a numeric card-sheet price or sheet capacity for this game. (low confidence) — https://www.thegamecrafter.com/make/pricing
- [statement] The Game Crafter bases bulk discounts on games in an order, not sheets or components in one game. Discounts vary with components; a headline maximum is not a guaranteed discount. Its bulk-pricing page includes a per-copy handling fee starting at $0.89, falling to $0.79 at 500 copies and $0.69 at 1000 copies. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-06-01) — https://help.thegamecrafter.com/article/84-bulk-pricing
- [statement] Panda describes two distinct approval samples: a near-final Pre-Production Copy of printed components before mass production, and a full Mass Production Copy before final assembly. This documents a supplier review process, not independently measured production quality or a guaranteed defect rate. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-06) — https://pandagm.com/our-process/
- [statement] Panda describes approval of the pre-production copy and component samples as the gate before mass production starts. This documents a contract-manufacturing approval step, not independent proof that production output will meet the buyer’s quality requirements. (low confidence) — https://pandagm.com/our-process/

## How it works

- [statement] Modeling prescription derived from relevant-cost analysis: within a constant-cost volume range, ownership cost equals incremental fixed ownership cost plus variable manufacturing cost per accepted game times accepted games; outsourcing cost equals its fixed setup cost plus delivered cost per accepted game times accepted games. The ownership crossover is the fixed-cost difference divided by the per-game variable-cost saving. It exists at positive volume only when those differences permit it. No numeric crossover is established here. (low confidence) — https://openstax.org/books/principles-managerial-accounting/pages/10-3-evaluate-and-determine-whether-to-make-or-buy-a-component · keywords: Card game manufacturing route choice and production economics · also: https://extension.missouri.edu/publications/g648
- [statement] For ownership cost indifference, equate the relevant total cost of making with the relevant total cost of buying at the same output. Algebraically, when unit costs are constant, incremental fixed cost divided by per-unit savings gives the crossover quantity. A positive ownership payback requires a positive saving; neither a machine price nor an output speed alone determines that quantity. This is a model derivation, not an observed game-production break-even volume. (medium confidence) — https://lmscontent.embanet.com/Media/UND/ACCT509/ACCT509-w01-m01/index.html · keywords: Card game manufacturing route choice and production economics · also: https://openstax.org/books/principles-managerial-accounting/pages/10-3-evaluate-and-determine-whether-to-make-or-buy-a-component
- [statement] Smartpress treats collating as grouping pieces into a specific sequence, but says collated sets ship unseparated unless a bundling option is selected, and belly bands are not automatic. Methodological implication: specify complete sets and physical set separation when comparing a trade-print route with an assembled-game service. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-06) — https://smartpress.com/support/product-faq/collated-printing-faq
- [statement] A manufacturing-cost markup alone does not determine a viable game price. Looney Labs recommends comparing similar games by box size, perceived quality and complexity; Frank West explains that a five-times multiplier can produce an unworkable first-game MSRP when small-run costs are high. (medium confidence) — https://faq.looneylabs.com/non-gameplay-questions/game-design-publishing · keywords: Card game manufacturing route choice and production economics · also: https://thecityofkings.com/news/how-to-price-your-game/
- [statement] Mayday says it may buy some additional copies directly from the factory when a publisher increases a print run. Its claim that this can improve manufacturing economics is conditional on a buyer agreement; it does not establish savings for an uncommitted larger run. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-06) — https://www.maydaygames.com/pages/board-game-publisher-overstock-program
- [statement] Epson’s ET-8550 guide distinguishes four paper sources. Its rear feed slot accepts thick media up to 1.3 mm, requires installation of the feed unit, and tells the operator to load paper when prompted. This is an attended handling requirement, not evidence of unattended batch throughput. (low confidence) — https://download4.epson.biz/sec_pubs/et-8550_series/useg/en/GUID-311A8905-0C48-4D76-8545-E44BAB44DB88.htm
- [statement] Duplo advertises the DSC-10/60i with ten bins, double-feed sensors, paper calibration and fine airflow adjustment, and up to 10,000 collated sets per hour when paired with its DBM-400STR stacker. Its stated input size starts at 4.1 by 5.8 inches. This is a document-sheet collating specification, not evidence of finished playing-card game output. (low confidence) — https://www.duplousa.com/product/dsc-10-60i-collator/
- [statement] Epson documents four ET-8550 paper sources; thick poster-board media up to 1.3 mm uses the rear paper feed slot, where loading waits for a control-panel message. The rear paper feeder is a different path, and Epson warns that some papers may not feed because of hardness or transparency. (low confidence) — https://download4.epson.biz/sec_pubs/et-8550_series/useg/en/GUID-311A8905-0C48-4D76-8545-E44BAB44DB88.htm

## Measurements and reference values

- [statement] The Game Crafter’s January 11, 2021 policy page describes its regular marketplace split as 70% of profit to the designer and 30% to the service. The percentages refer to profit, not to the full retail selling price; do not treat them as a universal distributor margin or a new negotiated quote. (low confidence) (verified as of 2021-01-11) — https://help.thegamecrafter.com/article/124-70-30-profit-split
- [statement] Mayday advertises purchasing selected excess game inventory for Mystery Boxes, but says it does not buy every title. It gives an indicative acquisition price around 90% off MSRP, with location-dependent variation. Treat this as one buyer’s contingent liquidation offer, not a guaranteed salvage value for unsold copies. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-06) — https://www.maydaygames.com/pages/board-game-publisher-overstock-program
- [statement] The Game Crafter’s ordinary marketplace documentation gives designers 70% of profit and the service 30%; its Sales page says it produces after a customer order and the designer remains responsible for promotion. This combines inventory exposure reduction with an ongoing demand-generation obligation. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2023-05-16) — https://help.thegamecrafter.com/article/124-70-30-profit-split · keywords: Card game manufacturing route choice and production economics · also: https://help.thegamecrafter.com/article/131-sales
- [statement] The same survey reports finishing constraints involving labor availability (43%), setup and makeready (35%), finishing speed relative to press speed (35%), and material handling (30%). These responses identify work to investigate; they do not supply minutes per game. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-06-04) — https://www.piworld.com/article/new-research-production-inkjets-next-bottleneck-is-finishing/

## Problems, failure modes and limitations

- [statement] In its historical account of 2021 conditions, Pandasaurus describes smaller print batches as more flexible, but also reports restocks failing to arrive when needed. Use that experience to scope replenishment risk; it does not supply current lead times or a guaranteed reorder schedule. (low confidence) — https://pandasaurusgames.com/blogs/pandasaurus-blog/the-business-of-board-games-everything-was-late-edition
- [statement] Recommended comparison convention: compute landed cost per accepted complete game as the relevant batch costs, including applicable freight, taxes, duties and rework, divided by accepted complete games. Record rejected or incomplete games separately. This is a proposed modeling convention derived from quote exclusions and the accounting text’s warning about quality-related replacements; no yield or failure rate is assumed. (medium confidence) — https://printninja.com/printing-prices/card-game-printing/ · keywords: Card game manufacturing route choice and production economics · also: https://openstax.org/books/principles-managerial-accounting/pages/10-3-evaluate-and-determine-whether-to-make-or-buy-a-component
- [statement] An automatic-duplex feature alone does not qualify an owned printer for thick card stock: Epson’s ET-8550 support page says automatic double-sided printing is unsupported on glossy, thick and certain matte papers. This limitation is model-specific, not a claim that every owned printer has the same restriction. (low confidence) — https://epson.com/faq/SPT_C11CJ21201~faq-00004fb-et8500_8550?faq_cat=faq-8796127602764
- [statement] Epson documents quality and handling qualifications for an owned printer: its scuff-reduction setting can reduce quality or slow printing, and manual duplex printing requires the ink to dry completely before the sheet is reloaded. Treat these as workflow constraints to verify on the intended stock, not measured production rates. (low confidence) — https://download4.epson.biz/sec_pubs/et-8550_series/useg/en/GUID-85133602-1F39-4AF0-9CAB-A0DC7C3C11A1.htm
- [statement] Unsold games tie up cash: Stonemaier explains that retailers pay for stock before selling it, and Mayday describes recovering capital from slow-moving publisher inventory. A lower unit manufacturing cost therefore needs a separate assessment of cash committed to unsold copies. (medium confidence) — https://stonemaiergames.com/the-math-of-tariffs/ · keywords: Card game manufacturing route choice and production economics · also: https://www.maydaygames.com/pages/board-game-publisher-overstock-program
- [statement] The Game Crafter’s Crowd Sale FAQ requires family-friendly content and manual approval. Its Crowd Sale economics cannot be assumed available for every party-game design. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-09-11) — https://help.thegamecrafter.com/article/401-crowd-sale-creator
- [statement] Epson warns that thick paper can scuff against the print head; its reduce-scuff setting may lower print quality or slow printing. A throughput trial must therefore retain the settings needed for acceptable output. (low confidence) — https://download4.epson.biz/sec_pubs/et-8550_series/useg/en/GUID-85133602-1F39-4AF0-9CAB-A0DC7C3C11A1.htm
- [statement] The Game Crafter explains that print-to-cut drift cannot be eliminated completely and recommends bleed and designs that make misalignment less visible. Treat this as a prepress and inspection requirement; bleed is not proof of duplex registration or a measured reject percentage. (low confidence) — https://help.thegamecrafter.com/article/392-drift
- [statement] For manual two-sided printing, Epson requires the first side to dry completely before reloading. Its thick-paper scuff remedy may slow printing or reduce print quality, so a faster setting is not a validated production rate for acceptable card stock. (low confidence) — https://download4.epson.biz/sec_pubs/et-8550_series/useg/en/GUID-85133602-1F39-4AF0-9CAB-A0DC7C3C11A1.htm

## Comparisons and alternatives

- [statement] PrintNinja says shipping costs vary with destination and residential versus commercial address type. Very large orders by volume or weight need a custom freight quote. US delivery scenarios therefore require actual addresses and package quantities. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-06) — https://printninja.com/global-shipping/
- [statement] Shopify’s reorder framework multiplies average sales rate by lead time and adds safety stock; its lead-time strategy includes manufacturing and supplier delivery. Apply consistent time units and project-specific demand rather than inventing a reorder threshold. (low confidence) — https://www.shopify.com/blog/safety-stock-vs-reorder-point
- [statement] PrintNinja labels standard ocean delivery uncertain and recommends extra schedule allowance. Reorder planning should allow for replenishment delays instead of assuming advertised transit is guaranteed. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-09-10) — https://printninja.com/help/ · keywords: Card game manufacturing route choice and production economics · also: https://printninja.com/shipping-methods/
- [statement] PrintNinja’s price list includes printing, binding, packaging and electronic proofs, but excludes shipping, sales tax and duties. Its standard hard-copy card proof is a separate $450 one-time option with specified stock, finish and packaging limitations. Treat the published deck price as a manufacturing benchmark rather than landed cost. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-02) — https://printninja.com/printing-prices/card-game-printing/
- [statement] MU Extension’s costing method measures a full batch, including materials and packaging; labor runs through placing finished output into inventory. Apply this method to the finished game rather than printer page speed: obtain actual total labor hours and accepted complete games before assigning labor cost per game. This is a proposed application, not measured card-production performance. (low confidence) — https://extension.missouri.edu/publications/g648
- [statement] A single linear ownership crossover is conditional: MU Extension notes that volume discounts can lower variable unit costs while extra equipment or property raises fixed costs. Recompute at actual quote tiers and capacity changes rather than extending one unit price across every quantity. (medium confidence) — https://extension.missouri.edu/publications/g648 · keywords: Card game manufacturing route choice and production economics · also: https://help.thegamecrafter.com/article/84-bulk-pricing
- [statement] Ownership cost parity and business sales break-even answer different questions. MU Extension defines sales break-even units as fixed costs divided by selling price per unit minus variable cost per unit; that revenue-based formula must not be used as the equipment-versus-outsourcing crossover. (medium confidence) — https://extension.missouri.edu/publications/g648 · keywords: Card game manufacturing route choice and production economics · also: https://openstax.org/books/principles-managerial-accounting/pages/10-3-evaluate-and-determine-whether-to-make-or-buy-a-component, https://www.sba.gov/counseling/plan-your-business/, https://lmscontent.embanet.com/Media/UND/ACCT509/ACCT509-w01-m01/index.html
- [statement] PrintNinja gives different inclusion scopes for posted prices and order quotes: its price list excludes shipping, sales tax and duties, while its order guidance says USD quotes for USA delivery include taxes and duties. Preserve those attributed scopes and verify the actual quote rather than adding taxes or duties twice. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-02) — https://printninja.com/printing-prices/card-game-printing/ · keywords: Card game manufacturing route choice and production economics · also: https://printninja.com/placing-an-order/
- [statement] The Game Crafter instructs quote users to enter the total number of cards of a given type for the whole game, including multiple decks. Count the complete game bill of materials rather than treating a stack as a whole game. (low confidence) — https://help.thegamecrafter.com/article/23-game-costs
- [statement] The Game Crafter says its custom-component quote excludes stock components. A complete game cost must add any applicable excluded parts instead of assuming the displayed custom-component total includes them. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-01-22) — https://help.thegamecrafter.com/article/23-game-costs
- [statement] Wiss recommends sensitivity analysis on maintenance assumptions, energy costs and utilization. For this game analysis, leave unmeasured operating inputs explicit and test alternative assumptions rather than inventing operating minutes, yield or equipment lifetime. (low confidence) — https://wiss.com/total-cost-of-ownership-manufacturing-equipment/
- [statement] Smartpress advises against Soft Touch laminate for playing cards because its tactile surface can make shuffling harder. This is supplier advice rather than independent shuffle testing; a premium-sounding finish should not be assumed to improve game handling. (low confidence) — https://smartpress.com/support/product-faq/collated-printing-faq
- [statement] Methodological inference: compare routes against a common physical specification and proof, rather than just a shared deck label. PrintNinja separates card stock, finish and packaging choices; Graphic Lab recommends a proof on its actual material, while Smartpress warns that a particular laminate can impair shuffling. (medium confidence) — https://printninja.com/printing-products/card-game-printing/ · keywords: Card game manufacturing route choice and production economics · also: https://www.graphiclabinc.com/custom-board-game-printing, https://smartpress.com/support/product-faq/collated-printing-faq
- [statement] Qualify local trade printing with a finished card sample rather than sheet-print capability alone (inference from historical operator evidence). Cole’s guide treats shuffleable cards as specialist production and recommends samples. In Koster’s 2013 comparison, his POD deck shuffled better than a copy-shop punch-out version, but had registration issues; the punch-out cards had rough perforated edges. These dated accounts do not establish current supplier performance. (medium confidence) — https://www.starfleetgames.com/fc/book/4-game_production-2.pdf · keywords: Card game manufacturing route choice and production economics · also: https://www.raphkoster.com/2013/09/05/a-little-card-game-prototype/
- [statement] Looney Labs advises allowing for distributor discounts of at least 60% off MSRP; Frank West described a 60–65% discount in his March 2022 first-game pricing example. Treat these as attributed channel-planning benchmarks rather than a guaranteed contract for this game. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2022-03-08) — https://faq.looneylabs.com/non-gameplay-questions/game-design-publishing · keywords: Card game manufacturing route choice and production economics · also: https://thecityofkings.com/news/how-to-price-your-game/
- [statement] The Game Crafter’s Bulk Pricing page, updated June 1, 2026, says discounts depend on the game components and some components retain fairly fixed costs at volume. Its bulk pricing counts complete games in one order, rather than sheets or components within one game; inspect the exact configured game instead of assuming a universal discount. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-06-01) — https://help.thegamecrafter.com/article/84-bulk-pricing
- [statement] Mayday’s overstock program is a limited salvage outlet, not assured full-price demand: it says typical purchases are 50–100 copies, reviews titles individually, and needs acquisition prices around 90% below MSRP, varying with location. This is Mayday’s commercial offer rather than an industry-wide liquidation rate. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-06) — https://www.maydaygames.com/pages/board-game-publisher-overstock-program
- [statement] Austin’s 2013 small-print-shop case used direct observation of a six-employee shop and recorded job steps, step durations, communication and material movement. This supports observing the complete workflow rather than timing only the print engine; its abstract is not a modern game-production benchmark. (low confidence) — https://repository.rit.edu/theses/5036/
- [statement] Morgana describes alternate-bin operation that permits reloading while the VF1008 runs by loading the same sheet in two bins; this uses duplicate bins and limits a single tower to four sheets per set in that mode. Continuous reloading therefore changes the usable collation configuration rather than eliminating loading work. (low confidence) — https://plockmaticgroup.com/kgs-acquisition/wp-content/uploads/2017/05/T10186_VF_1008_Op_Man.pdf

## Facts and statements

- [statement] UPS calculates dimensional weight from parcel volume divided by a rate-specific divisor and rounds fractional dimensional pounds upward. The guide lists 139 for Daily Rates and 166 for Retail Rates. Confirm the applicable rate agreement and final outer-carton dimensions. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-06) — https://www.ups.com/us/en/support/shipping-support/shipping-dimensions-weight
- [statement] UPS recommends a rigid shipping box and adequate cushioning. A game’s retail package therefore needs a separate transport-packaging decision; these guidelines do not establish a damage rate for this game. (low confidence) — https://www.ups.com/assets/resources/webcontent/en_US/Packaging_Guidelines.pdf
- [statement] PrintNinja’s card-game price table explicitly excludes shipping, sales tax and duties. Those production prices alone do not establish delivered cost. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-02) — https://printninja.com/printing-prices/card-game-printing/
- [statement] PrintNinja’s customs page says its pricing for US deliveries includes customs, duties and taxes. This is a vendor statement about its delivered service, not evidence that imported card games universally have zero import costs. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-20) — https://printninja.com/customs-policies-taxes-duties/
- [statement] PrintNinja’s published card-price table excludes shipping, sales tax, and duties; its help page says US-address quotes include taxes and duties in USD. Confirm the actual delivered quote boundary before adding import costs again. These are vendor statements, not an independent tariff determination. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-06) — https://printninja.com/printing-prices/card-game-printing/ · keywords: Card game manufacturing route choice and production economics · also: https://printninja.com/help/, https://printninja.com/customs-policies-taxes-duties/
- [statement] PrintNinja offers partial expediting: some copies travel by air and the remainder by ocean. It also warns that shipping times are approximate outside its guaranteed expedited service; model a split shipment as an option requiring its own quote. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-09-10) — https://printninja.com/shipping-methods/
- [statement] PrintNinja’s fulfillment page advertises storage at $0.08 per cubic foot per week. Treat this as its published affiliate rate, not a complete fulfillment price: the page separately calls for a custom shipping quote for diversion to EFS. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-04-27) — https://printninja.com/warehousing-and-fulfillment/
- [statement] EFS says it imposes no surcharge or higher fee solely for long-term storage. It also says it does not insure clients’ stored inventory. Storage aging charges and inventory insurance therefore need separate checks in a warehouse comparison. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-06) — https://www.efulfillmentservice.com/faq/storage/
- [statement] For a comparison model, keep parcel volume, warehouse volume over time and destination-specific delivery as separate inputs: UPS prices dimensional space, PrintNinja publishes storage per cubic foot per week, and PrintNinja says address type affects shipping. This is a modeling recommendation, not a measured finished-game cost. (medium confidence) — https://www.ups.com/us/en/support/shipping-support/shipping-dimensions-weight · keywords: Card game manufacturing route choice and production economics · also: https://printninja.com/warehousing-and-fulfillment/, https://printninja.com/global-shipping/
- [statement] A finished-game delivery model should separate manufacturing, receiving, handling, packaging, postage, and storage. PrintNinja excludes shipping from published manufacturing examples, while Laguna lists receiving, fulfillment, shipping boxes, postage, and storage separately. (medium confidence) — https://printninja.com/printing-prices/card-game-printing/ · keywords: Card game manufacturing route choice and production economics · also: https://lagunastudios.net/pages/fulfillment-rates
- [statement] Panda says custom shipping cartons and palletizing/shrink-wrapping or floor loading are included, but door-to-door shipping is excluded from manufacturing prices. This describes a manufacturer service, not independently demonstrated shipping protection. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-06) — https://pandagm.com/our-process/
- [statement] Laguna’s US card-game/tarot schedule lists receiving at $6 per box or $60 per pallet, fulfillment at $3.00–$3.50 per shipped box, and packaging boxes at $0.50–$1.50. Storage is $2–$10 per box/month or $20–$45 per pallet/month. Shipping is separate. Rates may change with fragility, dimensions, and quantity; this schedule is not a quote for the worked game. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-06) — https://lagunastudios.net/pages/fulfillment-rates
- [statement] Inventory carrying costs include capital opportunity cost, insurance, handling, and deterioration as well as storage. PrintNinja also warns that self-fulfillment requires warehousing, order work, tracking, shipping, and customer service. Home storage and self-fulfillment therefore need explicit costs. (medium confidence) — https://www.shopify.com/blog/inventory-carrying-costs · keywords: Card game manufacturing route choice and production economics · also: https://printninja.com/storage-and-fulfillment/
- [statement] Fanatics Collect warns that damp storage can warp cards, promote mold, and make cards stick together; excessive pressure can deform cards. This collector guidance identifies risks to evaluate for paper inventory, but supplies no finished-game warehouse specification or damage probability. (low confidence) — https://www.fanaticscollect.com/pages/how-to-protect-your-trading-card-collection-from-environmental-damage
- [statement] PrintNinja offers partial air expediting with the balance sent by ocean, and split delivery to multiple addresses. These are candidate ways to bridge an urgent need or divide warehouse and home stock; no project saving is quantified here. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-09-10) — https://printninja.com/shipping-methods/
- [statement] PrintNinja offers FOB by custom quote with shipment from Shenzhen port onward arranged by the customer, or EXW with customer-arranged factory pickup and full shipping. Model these responsibilities separately from delivered US quotes; applicable self-import duties remain unresolved. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-06) — https://printninja.com/help/
- [statement] A fulfillment provider’s Media Mail price menu does not establish that a party game qualifies. USPS describes games, including board games, as entertainment distinct from qualifying media. Establish postal eligibility for the actual product before using the menu’s media rate. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2018-07-01) — https://pe.usps.com/text/csr/ps-334.htm · keywords: Card game manufacturing route choice and production economics · also: https://lagunastudios.net/pages/fulfillment-rates
- [statement] MU Extension includes depreciation, repair and operating costs in equipment cost per hour and warns against counting the same expense again as a fixed cost. Equipment ownership may be allocated as fixed costs or through product operating costs, but those allocations must remain consistent. (low confidence) — https://extension.missouri.edu/publications/g648
- [statement] OpenStax’s make-or-buy analysis compares relevant costs: materials, labor and variable overhead differ between alternatives, while fixed costs that continue under either alternative do not determine the saving. Identify avoidable equipment and overhead costs before claiming an ownership advantage. (low confidence) — https://openstax.org/books/principles-managerial-accounting/pages/10-3-evaluate-and-determine-whether-to-make-or-buy-a-component
- [statement] Proposed landed-good-game accounting boundary: sum manufacturing, packaging, allocated setup, applicable inbound shipping, taxes and duties, and actual rework or replacement spending; divide by accepted complete games. Keep yield unknown until measured, and do not count replacement costs twice. This adapts batch input-output costing and the vendor’s explicit price exclusions; it is not a quoted landed price. (low confidence) — https://extension.missouri.edu/publications/g648 · keywords: Card game manufacturing route choice and production economics · also: https://printninja.com/printing-prices/card-game-printing/, https://openstax.org/books/principles-managerial-accounting/pages/10-3-evaluate-and-determine-whether-to-make-or-buy-a-component
- [statement] OpenStax says make-or-buy decisions also require quality, delivery, supplier-price and available-capacity assessment. A cheaper nominal per-unit figure alone does not establish an economically equivalent finished product. (low confidence) — https://openstax.org/books/principles-managerial-accounting/pages/10-3-evaluate-and-determine-whether-to-make-or-buy-a-component
